articles.title: The root-to-tip revolution! An A-Z of how to eat plants in full – for extra flavour, fibre and savings
articles.description: If you discard the peels, skins, stalks and seeds when consuming fruit and vegetables you are missing out on a lot of value. Here’s what to incorporate into your diet – and what to avoid Do you peel your potatoes, deseed your squash and core your cauliflower? A study by King’s College London, published last month in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, found that people who routinely discard peels, skins, stalks and seeds when preparing fruit and vegetables are missing out on a valuable source of dietary fibre. Ten out of the 12 types of produce the researchers analysed had higher levels of fibre in the scraps than in the flesh. Eating these often overlooked parts could help address the global dietary fibre deficit and tackle food waste, they say. Here, experts share their advice on how to cook and eat “root to tip”. articles.title: World: COP31: FAO welcomes endorsement of Antalya Action Plan on Integrated Fire Management
articles.description: Countries turning wildfire commitments into action 16/11/2026 Antalya, Türkiye – The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) today welcomed the endorsement by 23 countries of an initiative to turn growing political commitments on wildfire resilience into practical action on the ground at the 2026 UN Climate Change Conference (COP31). The Antalya Action Plan on Integrated Fire Management is spearheaded by the Republic of Türkiye in its COP31 Presidency and co-led by Brazil and the Republic of Korea, with support from FAO through the Global Fire Management Hub and from the Forest & Climate Leaders’ Partnership. The country-led, voluntary plan aims to translate political commitments on wildfire resilience into coordinated action through greater collaboration, shared learning and expanding practical solutions. “The scale and complexity of wildfire risks mean that countries cannot solve this challenge in isolation,” said Zhimin Wu, FAO Assistant Director-General and Director of the Forestry Division. “The value of the Antalya Action Plan is in connecting very different experiences - from prevention and community action to technology, landscape management and international cooperation - so that countries can learn from one another and act faster,” he added. A shared response to a growing threat Wildfires are becoming more frequent and more severe, driven by climate change and changes in land use, with extreme fire events projected to increase by up to 50 percent by the end of this century. On average, 261 million hectares of land was affected by fire annually in 2007–2019, almost half of which was forested, according to the Global Forest Resources Assessment 2025. Smoke and fire-related pollution can cross borders, affecting human health, biodiversity and ecosystem services. Recent international commitments – including the Istanbul Report on Integrated Fire Management, the G7 Kananaskis Wildfire Charter, the Belém Call to Action on Integrated Fire Management and Wildfire Resilience and the UNEA-7 resolution on strengthening the global management of wildfires – reflect a growing consensus that wildfires demand urgent, coordinated action and a shift from reactive firefighting towards prevention and preparedness. The Action Plan aims to turn this consensus into practice. By giving participating countries a shared community to exchange the measures they are taking to improve wildfire management, learn from one another and benefit from tools, measures and initiatives that already exist, it aims to offer a mechanism for the international community to move from fragmented efforts towards a more coordinated and effective global response. The plan is structured around four outcomes: strengthening international cooperation, using science and local knowledge to prevent and reduce wildfire risks, managing landscapes adaptively, and improving access to resources for integrated fire management and wildfire resilience, especially in developing countries. Supporting countries from commitment to practice The development and launch of the Antalya Action Plan was supported by the Global Fire Management Hub and the Forest & Climate Leaders’ Partnership. FAO hosts the Secretariat of the Global Fire Management Hub, a multi-partner initiative that was launched by FAO and the UN Environment Programme in 2023. The Global Fire Management Hub Secretariat will serve as the Secretariat for the Action Plan, connecting participating countries with other partners, networks and Fire Hub activities to strengthen the implementation of integrated fire management. The Global Fire Management Hub connects expertise, guidance, data, tools and networks, while its partnerships and working groups support practical collaboration and knowledge exchange. Partners launched the Action Plan today at the COP31 event “High-Level Dialogue on Technology and Innovation for Integrated Fire Management and Wildfire Resilience” in Antalya, Türkiye.
